cases.answer: before anything else the client opens a TCP connection to the server, that's the three way handshake, it sends a SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK and the client sends an ACK, so both sides agree on sequence numbers. after that TCP makes sure the bytes arrive in order and resends anything that gets lost. that setup costs a full round trip, so if the server is far away or overloaded you see it as a connect timeout, and that's why keep-alive and reusing connections matter.

a request has a method like GET or POST, a path, headers and maybe a body, and the response has a status code, headers and a body. the method is a promise: GET should only read, so caches and proxies can store it and clients can retry it safely. if you use GET to delete something, a cache or a retry can run it again, or a crawler can trigger it. and the status code tells the client what happened, like 201 created or 404, so you shouldn't return 200 for an error.
the request has a method like GET POST PUT DELETE, some headers, and the response comes back with a status code like 200 or 404.
GET and POST are basically the same, POST just hides the parameters, so it doesn't matter which one you use for changing data.

HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. TLS gives you encryption, so nobody in the middle can read the data, and it authenticates the server with a certificate signed by a CA, so you know you're really talking to api.example.com. the cost is the handshake, the client and server agree on keys and check the certificate before any data, which adds one or two round trips, so session resumption and keeping connections open help latency.

the client says what kind of action it wants, a read or a create or a change, then some extra info lines, and then the content. the server answers with a number saying how it went, the two hundreds mean fine, the four hundreds mean you did something wrong. the read kind is supposed to change nothing, because things in between like caching layers will save it and replay it, and a client that lost the answer will just send it again, so if your read kind actually deletes stuff you can delete twice.
